title: "Bench hardware"
description: "What to build, and what to buy"

---

A board running `UsbIo` is an instrument, not a bench. Everything between the
sensor and the pin — and in some cases the pin itself — still has to be
added, and what you add depends on what you plan to measure. This page
organises the bench hardware into three cumulative cost tiers, maps each
experiment to the tier and items it needs, and says what belongs on a
breadboard and what does not.

## Three tiers

Each tier adds to the one before it; nothing bought for tier 1 becomes
redundant once the bench reaches tier 3.

### Tier 1 — board, reference, meter

- A supported board — see [Supported boards](../setup/boards.qmd)
- USB cable, and a hub where the board needs one
- A voltage reference IC, for a known calibration point
- A digital multimeter, better than the board and with a stated
  specification — see [S1](../experiments/S1-daq-static/index.qmd)
- Breadboard, resistors and wires, for a divider calibration point

Enough for S1, and for anything that only needs a resistance reading — no
signal generator, no data acquisition card beyond the board itself.

### Tier 2 — signal generator, conditioning board

- A signal generator, for driving a known waveform into the board
- A [signal conditioning board](conditioning-board.qmd): an offset-and-scale
  stage, resistive dividers, an instrumentation amplifier, a buffer

Adds S2, and any experiment whose sensor's native output range does not
already sit inside the ADC's input window — which, per S1, is most of them.

### Tier 3 — filter stage, thermal rig, beam rig

- An [anti-alias filter stage](filter-stage.qmd)
- A [thermal rig](thermal-rig.qmd): stirred bath, ice bath, reference
  thermometer, sensor-mounting hardware
- A [cantilever beam rig](beam-rig.qmd): the shared mechanical specimen,
  strain gauges, a Hall sensor and target, a mount for an accelerometer

Completes S3 and the mechanical strand, and the thermal experiments that need
the rig itself rather than just a resistance reading.

Costs are collected, per item, in the [bill of materials](bom.qmd) — none
are recorded yet; that page explains why it is still worth reading before
they are.

## What each experiment needs

@tbl-hw-experiments is built directly from each experiment's own front
matter (`experiment.needs`, `experiment.tier`), which is the authoritative
list — this page does not duplicate numbers that live there and could drift
out of sync with them.

| Experiment | Tier | Hardware needed |
|---|:--:|---|
| [S1](../experiments/S1-daq-static/index.qmd) — Static DAQ characterization | [1]{.tier .tier-1} | Voltage reference IC, DMM |
| [S2](../experiments/S2-daq-dynamic/index.qmd) — Dynamic DAQ characterization | [2]{.tier .tier-2} | Signal generator, [conditioning board](conditioning-board.qmd) |
| [S3](../experiments/S3-aliasing-filtering/index.qmd) — Aliasing, conditioning and filtering | [3]{.tier .tier-3} | Signal generator, conditioning board, [filter stage](filter-stage.qmd) |
| [T1](../experiments/T1-temperature-static/index.qmd) — Static temperature calibration | [2]{.tier .tier-2} | [Thermal rig](thermal-rig.qmd), reference thermometer, conditioning board |
| [T2](../experiments/T2-temperature-dynamic/index.qmd) — Dynamic temperature response | [2]{.tier .tier-2} | Thermal rig, reference thermometer |
| [T3](../experiments/T3-long-term-stability/index.qmd) — Long-term stability and drift | [3]{.tier .tier-3} | Insulated box, a bench host that stays on |
| [M1](../experiments/M1-strain-load/index.qmd) — Strain gauges and load cell | [3]{.tier .tier-3} | [Beam rig](beam-rig.qmd), load cell, instrumentation amplifier, reference masses |
| [M2](../experiments/M2-hall-displacement/index.qmd) — Hall-effect displacement | [3]{.tier .tier-3} | Beam rig, micrometer stage, linear Hall sensor |
| [M3](../experiments/M3-vibration/index.qmd) — Vibration and modal analysis | [3]{.tier .tier-3} | Beam rig, accelerometer, strain gauge channel |

: Hardware required by experiment, from each experiment's own front matter {#tbl-hw-experiments}

Two entries look out of place next to the tier framing above: T1 and T2 are
tier-2 experiments that need the thermal rig, which is described here
alongside tier-3 hardware. That is not a mistake — the rig itself (a vessel,
a stirrer, an ice bucket) is cheap, while a signal generator and a
conditioning board are not, and tier is tracking cost and build effort, not
which page of this section happens to document the hardware.

## Breadboard, or a soldered board {#sec-hw-breadboard}

Digital I/O, a quick resistive divider for a calibration point, a first check
that a sensor responds at all — a breadboard is fine for these, and faster to
change than solder. The analog stages of the conditioning and filter boards
are a different case:

::: {.callout-important}
## Why the analog stages should not stay on a breadboard

- **Contact resistance.** A breadboard's spring contacts are not a soldered
  joint: their resistance is neither zero nor stable, and it moves with
  vibration, oxidation and how firmly the wire was pushed in. A few tens of
  milliohms of drifting resistance is invisible on a digital line and is a
  direct, time-varying error on a divider ratio or a bridge arm.
- **Stray capacitance.** The strips and the long, unshielded jumpers common
  on a breadboard add capacitance to ground that is neither small nor
  specified. Combined with the source impedance of a divider or a
  high-impedance sensor, it forms an unintended low-pass pole exactly where
  the [filter stage](filter-stage.qmd) is trying to place one on purpose —
  and the two interact in ways that are not designed for.
- **Thermoelectric junctions.** Every place two dissimilar metals touch — a
  nickel-plated spring contact against a tinned jumper wire — is a
  thermocouple junction, generating a Seebeck EMF of order microvolts to tens
  of microvolts per kelvin of local temperature difference. That is
  comparable to, or larger than, the LSB voltages [S1](../experiments/S1-daq-static/index.qmd)
  measures, and it responds to draughts and to a hand held near the board.
  A soldered joint has the same physics but a far smaller, far more stable
  EMF, because the junction and its temperature stay fixed.

None of these three matters for a digital pin toggling between 0 V and
$V_\mathrm{ref}$. All three matter for a stage whose entire purpose is to
preserve a signal to better than a percent.
:::

Build the conditioning and filter stages on a soldered board — perfboard is
enough; it does not need to be a fabricated PCB — and keep the breadboard for
whatever still changes between sessions.
